utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I note that the witness is going to be coming in shortly; however, Mr. Topolski has alerted me to something that he would like to raise with the Chamber which I think is of some importance. So if my examination could be delayed for a moment so he can raise this issue with the Court, I would appreciate it, as I think would all Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: At a meeting with my co-counsel Mr. Powles --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're in open session. Is that going to be an issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I would like to be in private session for the purpose of this application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'll move to private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I represent the third accused in this case, whose name is Isak Musliu. Isak Musliu, during the war, had the name Qerqizi. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions. I'm going to try and keep my questions short. If you do not understand me, please stop me and I will try again. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man you were told who was called Qerqizi beat you and beat others, did he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not say that we were beaten, but he told me his real name, because he was related to him. But Qerqizi beat us all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The man you were told was called Qerqizi always wore a mask, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Qerqizi regularly wore a mask. And he knew him. I knew him as Qerqizi. He knew him from before, and he told me the real name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said in this room --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, without me touching it, my microphone keeps going off. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to advise you that because of voice distortion, that happens. So each time you speak again after somebody else, you must press again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Powles is now on microphone duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A very wise manoeuvre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, in this room, you said Qerqizi always wore a mask.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was, you said yesterday, of medium build; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, medium.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately 170 centimetres tall you said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were told he was called Qerqizi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's how I knew him, as Qerqizi, for the whole 28 days I stayed in the stable.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to put the name of the person who he told us yesterday told him that, and for this purpose only may we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 29th of November, when you came to The Hague, you told somebody from the Office of the Prosecutor that Qerqizi wore a black uniform; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regularly, yes, a black uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told investigators from the ICTY, from this court, that other men also wore black uniforms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Military police of the KLA, whoever they was -- they were from them, they had black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told investigators from this court that some men wore black uniforms and had the letters PU on their arms and on their caps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean at that time or earlier than that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's a very good question. My question to you, sir, is this: Is it correct that you told investigators that when you were in the camp in Lapusnik, men wore black uniforms with PU on their arms and on their caps? Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand. If I would understand, I would have told you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I'll try again. It's not your fault if you don't understand me, it's my fault. All right? I am looking here at the statement that you made, and you made it in October of 2002. Do you understand? That's what I'm looking down at now, all right? I think you need to answer if you understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember ever saying that. I am repeating. It's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course it has, but I'm going to read to you very slowly from page U0031203 one sentence written by you. "They," and the they you are referring to are two men called Shala and Murrizi, "wore black uniforms and had PU for "policia ushtarake," military police, "on their arms and caps." I have just read that line from your witness statement. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can hear you very well. I have seen PU, but I don't think I've said about Qerqizi, that he had PU, only that his clothes were black.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, in the camp, see men wearing black uniforms with PU on their arms or on their caps? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember if I've seen there in there, the letters PU, in the stable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you have said that you did see this in a statement that you made, it's probably true, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the stable, I can't remember if I saw them, whether they had PU or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I didn't say stable, I said statement. If it's in your statement, it's true, isn't it? You wouldn't lie in a statement, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have tried to tell the truth and not to lie, and I've tried to say only the truth. And I'm not lying now, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were many soldiers and guards at this place, were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were soldiers around, but Shala was the guard all the time for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You will leave this witness box much quicker, I expect, if you just answer my questions and not volunteer information. Do you understand me? Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you agree with the estimate that there may have been as many as 50 soldiers or guards at this camp from time to time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember. There have been many soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can speak the truth. If you give me the floor, I can say the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The men who were acting as soldiers were of different sizes, different heights, and different ages, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were soldiers, because I could hear them speaking outside, but I was inside. I did not count them, how many there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course you didn't count them. My question was: Because there were a number of them, they all were different heights and sizes and ages, weren't they? It's obvious. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said it once, and I will say it again. There were many soldiers. There was a headquarters there, but inside there we were chained. And Shala came there. We saw him, and Qerqizi came to beat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One of the soldiers there was called Murrizi, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw on the television that Murrizi had been killed, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I saw. And the photograph, it looked familiar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You recognised him as soon as you saw his photograph on the television, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I thought -- yes. I saw him on the television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Murrizi's real name was Besim Beli, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember for the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Murrizi was a man who let you see his face at the place, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Murrizi did not wear a mask.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the last day, this man Murrizi told you that you were going to be free, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He came and opened the door and said, "Don't try to leave. Don't try to escape. We will tell you where to go." He unchained us. From the chains.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when he did that, as usual, he did not have a mask on covering his face, did he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was without a mask.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while we're on the subject of masks, I want to show you a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: This is a photograph, Your Honours, from Prosecution Exhibit 18. Copies have been circulated, I hope. We can have it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to look at this photograph, please, U0032776.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Excuse me, Mr. Topolski. Your Honour, would it be possible for the witness to actually have it in front of him because of his eyesight and then it can go on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In fact, what I can -- to assist my learned friend, we can put it on Sanction so everybody will see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Very well. Let's have it on Sanction. I used the wrong terminology, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see the photos, but I don't know this person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's no one in that photograph you know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's no one in that photograph that you know; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want you to look at the three people who are standing up and look at their masks, and I want you to tell us, please, about the mask that Qerqizi used to wear. Was it like any of those masks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The masks were all black in the -- so in the photo, they were all in black. They are all in black.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the mask that Qerqizi wore a black mask?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's how we came in black -- he came in black.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at the three people standing in the photograph. Did the mask that Qerqizi wore look the same as any of those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I told you, in the photo they are all in black. I cannot tell. I cannot tell anything from the photo. I just see three soldiers here in hats, in masks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are in fact five soldiers in this photograph wearing masks. Three of them are standing; two of them are seated. Can you see that? Look at the photograph on the table in front of you, not at the screen, if it's easier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I seen the photo that the masks are black and they were all wearing black masks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are they the masks like the ones Qerqizi wore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether theirs were like Qerqizi's, but the clothes were black and they were wearing black masks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see that two of the women sitting on the right of the photograph seem to have the letters PU on their arms? Do you see that in the photograph in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you, please, is it your evidence that you saw uniforms like that in the place in Lapusnik when you were being held there? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember for the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back for a moment to talk about Murrizi, the man who released you on the last day. You can forget the photograph now. You can put it away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Perhaps it could be taken from him so it doesn't distract. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm back now, sir, asking you about Murrizi. All right? Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good. Were you watching television at all last year, February 2003, when these defendants first came before this court? Did you see that on television last year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw on TV everything that -- what was occurring after the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was about this court, this place, The Hague, and Fatmir Limaj and others coming before the court, which would have been on television.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have time to -- it watch them on TV all the time in the trial. Sometimes I'd watch, sometimes not, but I remember myself watching this particular thing on TV.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that they were saying that Murrizi was here last February in The Hague in 2003? Did you know they were saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember this. I do not remember anything about Murrizi being here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He could not have been here, the real Murrizi, in 2003 because he was dead. That's right, isn't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know he is dead, but that's how it seemed to me from that photo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you recognise the man they were calling Murrizi here when you watch the television about the case last year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you tell anyone they'd got the wrong man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't remember myself saying that to anyone, but I saw that this wasn't the real Murrizi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw this was not the real Murrizi, but you did nothing about it. Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I saw him on TV, I said to myself, "This -- this is not Murrizi." I remember -- I remember this. He wasn't Murrizi. He wasn't his body build or anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. The real Murrizi was dead?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The real Murrizi was dead. Why did you stay silent when you saw that they had the wrong Murrizi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw that that was mistake, and this I can say here again. It wasn't the real Murrizi, that one that I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your purpose, sir, to tell us the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I swore in here, and I'm here to tell the truth, but if I can't remember, I can't remember. Things that I know, I'm stating here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it matter to you that an innocent man may be convicted? Does that matter to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I'm telling the truth here. Of course I'd regret very much if somebody who was not guilty was sentenced here. I can tell you only what I saw. I am telling you what I myself have experienced and nothing -- nothing but that. I -- I can forget things, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There will be a redaction. We will go to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm not going to mention any other names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We can remain in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, please. Your Honour, microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: My apologies. I forgot to apply to go into private session when I put the name. My fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will redact that name, and we can now go back to open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Qerqizi, you have said before, was a very wicked man. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was always very aggressive, from the very first time when I saw him in Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was this, this Qerqizi, a very violent man, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Qerqizi beat us every time. He was aggressive. He did everything, almost everything to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A man you will never forget.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I can't forget that man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 16th of January, 2002, you sat down with a gentleman called Kereakes from Chicago, and he was an investigator. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, now I can't tell. I don't remember simply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had a friend with you who was helping you with translation. That friend was speaking German. Do you remember now what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if you are talking about the first time. In the beginning, I mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember this, but I do not remember the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this was the 16th of January, 2002, and was the first time that you sat down with investigators. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the first time, but I can't remember the year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was January 2002, some four and a half years after you had left the place at Lapusnik; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, that's true, but I can't tell you about the year. I do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to use, I hope, very simple words about this interview, and I hope that you are going to be able to answer me either yes or no to each of these questions. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that interview with Mr. Kereakes, you gave him a lot of information, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I talked to him the first time. There was an interpreter there. I know what you're talking about. I was interpreting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about places to him, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. About Lapusnik, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about things that happened, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You even remembered part of the registration number of certain vehicles that were involved, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, yes. No, I don't remember this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you you did. At page 03231249 at the end of the first paragraph you refer to a vehicle with a Serbian registration number on two occasions. So I'm telling you you did remember registration numbers. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, this didn't happen. I do not remember myself saying anything about the Serbian registration plates, and I don't remember talking about this fact at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that you did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can I just interject at this stage? I think to be fair to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that. I didn't say this. I don't remember myself mentioning this thing about the registration plates or the number of the registration plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Without alerting the witness, Mr. President, to what Mr. Topolski is talking about, I think if the section is actually read out to him in closed session, it might actually refresh his memory, because it's talking about vehicles that he knows, but just reading it out like that, I don't think the witness is going to remember. It's a suggestion anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I think it's a very helpful one and I'm grateful for it. I was actually going to put the statement in Albanian in front of him. But may I then ask to go into closed session and I shall read the two lines from the end of the first paragraph on the page I identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Closed session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hope, sir, that you will take it from me that in this interview with Mr. Kereakes, and I'm not going to mention any of them, you have mentioned no fewer than the names of 16 different people. I know it's hard for you to remember, but will you take my word for it? I've counted them, 16 different names. Do you accept that or do you not accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember mentioning 16 different names. If you're talking about people who were there with me or with whom we were released or how many were -- were staying after we were released, then it's a different question, but I do not remember this fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not going to mention any names. You gave the names of people who took you and people you were with where you were taken. Do you accept that or do you not accept that? And if you like, I can show you the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only -- only the -- if we're talking about the first time when the registration plates were mentioned. But I do not know the numbers on the registration plate. I don't know about the names.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were here with this investigator because you had decided to tell your story. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't understand you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had decided to be brave and to speak, hadn't you? That's why you were there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I didn't decide to be brave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You wanted the authorities to know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You wanted the authorities to know what had happened to you and to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. others. That's why you were there speaking to the investigator, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can tell only the truth. It's not that I decided to become brave or anything or invent things that didn't happen. What I have experienced I've already stated here, what I went through and what I know only. I'm telling you only my sufferings here. In one of my arms, I have the chain marks still.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why, why did you not tell the investigator the name Qerqizi in this first meeting? The most violent man, the worst man, the terrible man, why didn't you mention his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember anybody asking me those questions, the questions you are asking now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were next to meet investigators nearly two months later, on the 13th of March, 2002. We have before us a record of a meeting that you had, and you took them to a place. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you're talking about the mountains, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Page 0323-1269 for anybody's reference. It seems during that day you spent with investigators again you do not mention the terrible man Qerqiz. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember anybody asking me about Qerqiz or about these things, otherwise -- I don't remember anybody asking me that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first time that you mention the name Qerqiz is at your third meeting with investigators, a week later, March the 20th, 2002.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, again, I hope you'll take it from me. I'm looking at a document 03231271, a statement made by you in which, for the first time, the name Qerqiz is mentioned. Did you remember now? Did they ask you about him or did you remember to speak his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the moment, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had another meeting on the 1st of April now, 2002. This is meeting number four. And I'm going to ask you now about something you've not spoken of yet. In this meeting, 0323-1282, you talk about two female soldiers taking someone away. Do you remember telling investigators about this? Don't mention the person's name. Just answer my question yes or no. Do you remember speaking about two female UCK soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can mention the names here if you're talking about these two females that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Because it may involve a victim, perhaps we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the investigator that someone was beaten by the sister of Qerqizi. You told them that because somebody else had given you that information. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't remember saying anything about Qerqiz's sister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you did. And you did it because you are prepared to put someone's name in the frame simply because of what other people tell you. That's what you've done here, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. My -- I don't believe I have spoken anything -- I have said anything about Qerqiz's sister. If I had, then I would admit it. I -- what I know, I know. What I don't know, I don't know it. But I haven't said this. Six years have already passed, and I might forget things. What I know, I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I know is, sir, is that you have --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I know is what I read from your words, from your witness statement dated the 1st of April, and I shall read the line to you: "As far as I know, one of the female soldiers is from Racak. She is the sister of Qerqiz, and she is working now as a KPS officer in Ferizaj." You --

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could Mr. Topolski, Your Honour, please read the last sentence of that statement, because I think it will become a little clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And could we go into private session for me to do so. And I was going to anyway. I was trying to break it up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The very last time you met with investigators to talk about this case before coming into this room was on -- when you arrived in this city. Do you remember? At the back end of November, a few days ago. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you put the question one more time, please? I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly. The last time, I suggest the sixth time, on which you sat down and spoke with investigators about this case was just a few days ago when you arrived here in The Hague. Do you remember sitting down with members of the Office of the Prosecutor and talking about your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we talked, but I don't know what about, what's in question here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll come to the questions. I just want to ask you if you remember sitting and talking to them, and you do. You talked to them about Qerqizi, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we talked about Qerqizi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was the first time that you were trying to give a description of Qerqizi, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean here or earlier?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I mean here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is when you told them that you found out that his name was Isak Musliu, and you found that out from a man called --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I think I have said this in open session, but we'll go into private for an abundance of caution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about whether you have seen the man Isak Musliu or heard the man Isak Musliu in the last few years. You've already told us you have seen on television this trial. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As for Qerqizi, I've seen him on TV.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen any photographs of him in the papers, newspapers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Because I -- my sight is not very well, and I don't get them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what a calendar is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think I know what's a calendar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you seen a picture of Qerqizi on a calendar for sale in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I didn't have a chance to see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think what we can, sir, agree about is this, that the only reason you call Qerqizi Isak Musliu is because others have told you that is his name. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I told you from whom I heard his real name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about another name that you mentioned yesterday, Tamuli. Do you remember speaking about Tamuli yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that a little.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tamuli is a famous name in Kosovo now, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never heard of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tamuli was a martyr. His death is remembered every year in Kosovo, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know he's a hero, but I don't go there. I never go there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, in 1998, the man Tamuli was not known as Tamuli. He had another name. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know him just as Tamuli. I do not know of him having some other name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1998, because he is dark skinned and for no other reason, he was known as Mujahedini. That was his nickname. Have you heard that before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean they would call Tamuli Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. If you saw him in Lapusnik in 1998, he would not have been known as Tamuli. He wasn't called that until much later. So I'm asking you, are you sure he was Tamuli in 1998, or is that something else someone's told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know from whom I heard this, but people would call him Tamuli. I'm in the aware of any other name for him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We know that the last day you could have been in this place in Lapusnik was the 26th of July, 1998. You told us that Qerqiz came to you every night except the last week. Is that the truth? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Qerqiz would come there sometimes at night, sometime during the day, and there wouldn't pass a night without him beating us. This is the truth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Transcript, my page 38, line 25, yesterday you told Mr. Cayley, the gentleman sitting over there to your right, that he came every night except the last week. Now, what I want to ask you is, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, every night he would come and would be beat us. Whenever he wasn't busy fighting, he would come there during the day or during the night and he would beat us, except for the last week.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by "week," do you mean seven days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not -- not a full week. I would say last days maybe. Three days maybe, not more than that. So every day or night. He wouldn't come during the day. He would come at night. And he would curse our mothers. He would kick us. He would punch us. Our -- our lower extremities were in blood. I still have the marks, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't doubt, sir, that these things may have happened to you. The question is who did them. You see, the man I represent wasn't in Lapusnik for the seven days up to the 26th of July. He was fighting elsewhere. So he couldn't have come to see you to beat you. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. In question here are three days. So when the --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the Serb offensive started and when they were moving towards Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we need to understand that when you say the last week, in fact what you mean is the last three days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before I was released. Before I was released to go from the barn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the war, did you hear Qerqiz, Isak Musliu, giving an interview on the radio about the battles he fought? Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that Isak Musliu --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that Isak Musliu was in the military police in the Nerodimje zone after the war? Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's all I ask this witness. I apparently gave the wrong transcript reference, if it matters. On the corrected version perhaps it's 28 and not 38. I apologise. I was looking at the uncorrected transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: For the reference to the last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness, can you hear me? Witness, good afternoon. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Now, I have very little for you, so you will be released by the Presiding Judge very soon. I have a few questions for you. You were asked yesterday by Mr. Mansfield, counsel for Fatmir Limaj, the following question: "Had you ever been to Lapusnik before the war?" And your answer was, "I went there regularly." Now, the question I have for you is this: Before the war, how regularly, how often did you go to Lapusnik, the village of Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Lapusnik village, I was not there at all before the war. I was going through village of Lapusnik in my tractor once a week maybe. I would go to Orllat, which is close to Lapusnik, and I would pass through that road there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: So you -- prior to the war --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Prior to the war, you passed through the village of Lapusnik once a week; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How well do --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mike, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: How well do you know the village of Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Lapusnik quite well. I've told you I've gone through that place there, and I know the place. I've been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for the witness. The only matter that I would address and this is on -- I should do it with the witness here. I showed the witness a photograph from the Prosecutor's Exhibit 6, which is the photograph of the stable, and I quoted the ERN number, and this is on page 80 of the draft transcript. I'll read out my question because it's probably a different page in the repaginated version, and I said the following: "The witness is pointing to the right-hand back wall of the stable in U0083764 when he is indicating where Veseli was located in the stable." In fact, the correct number is U0083674. So I simply reversed a number, and indeed I think my colleagues can check that photograph and they'll see that it is the correct number now. I see Mr. Khan is nodding, so I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. That accords with our numbering as well. Sir, I must tell you that your questioning has finished. You will be pleased to know that there is no further questioning. The Chamber would like to thank you for coming to The Hague and for the assistance that you have given to us. You are now excused and free to go back to your home. People outside will assist you with those arrangements. In just a moment, you will be able to leave there and go out to the witness area. Thank you. You're free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, are you ready with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We are ready, Your Honour, to proceed with the next witness. He is going to be led in his evidence by my colleague Mr. Black. You will be pleased to hear that this witness will be in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If Your Honours could excuse me for two or three minutes, I will be back here to sit in with Mr. Black, but I have to attend to something upstairs. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cayley. The next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. It's Mr. Bakrac, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Obviously you can hear me in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you take the affirmation card that is offered to you now and read aloud the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you would sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May it please the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, can you understand me as well?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Are you comfortable where you are?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'll ask you if at any time you don't understand something that I ask you, one of my questions, please tell me, and I'll try to rephrase it or put it another way. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Now, I would just like to mention, except when we go into what we'll call private session, I'll ask you not to mention the country in which you currently reside. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, before I ask you questions about your background and the events that happened in 1998, I'd like to briefly go over the statements that you have given before you came here today. First, do you recall that you were interviewed by an investigator of the ICTY in January of 2003?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you make a signed statement at that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And have you been given a chance to review that statement and make any necessary corrections?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Between the time that you made that statement and when you came here to The Hague to testify, did you meet with any representatives of the ICTY before you arrived in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But since you arrived in The Hague, you and I have met on a couple of occasions to discuss your testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Before meeting with the ICTY investigator in 2003, had you ever given a statement to any organisation about your experiences in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately after the events concerned, to the International Organisation for Humanitarian Law.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I would like to show the witness a document with the ERN U0031082 to U0031092.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, I'd just like you to look at that document for a moment. Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is that the statement to the international organisation that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. That is this first statement I gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And when did you give that statement, what date?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: On the 2nd of August, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. And where did the interview take place, in which country?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: In Serbia, in Belgrade, in a small place called Grocka near Belgrade. That is my wife's birthplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned that you gave this statement shortly after the events concerned. Were the events fresh in your mind at the time you made that statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, quite fresh.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to review this statement and to make any corrections?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to read over this statement?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Not until I came here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And when you came here, did you read it?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, is this an accurate account of what happened to you in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, it is an accurate account.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this be marked as the next Prosecution Exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On what basis, Mr. Black?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence have suggested that this case is fabricated, that the witnesses made up their evidence after, sometime after the events. We would say that this is a practically contemporaneous statement. It was made on the 2nd of August, 1998, and it's probative evidence that at least he didn't subsequently fabricate his story because, in fact, he told it to this organisation on the 2nd of August, 1998. On that basis I would seek its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: To answer, without turning to my right, is no. It may be marked at the moment for identification. It has been identified. Should there be suggestion of recent invention or some such, it may become of significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just a moment while the record keeps up.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P77 ID, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Not an exhibit, marked for identification only.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, other than the two statements that we just discussed, have you given any other statements about your experience in 1998?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were you ever interviewed by the Serbian authorities about your experience?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: The day after I was released, at the State Security Centre in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Have you spoken with any of the other victims since you were released?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about your son? Have you discussed the substance of your testimony with him?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: No. We did not discuss the substance of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And, sir, last question on this topic. Have you watched any part of this trial either at home on television or here since you've been in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: No. I just glanced at newspaper articles, things like that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I'll now ask you a few questions about your background. Where were you born?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: In Brezice, Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: On what date?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: The 11th of November, 1950.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can say, as far as the preliminary matters are concerned and the background up to 1998, I have no objections at all if my friend seeks to lead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Khan. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I join.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a view that's shared by all? Thank you. That may speed things up, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, do you consider yourself a Yugoslav?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And do you practice the Orthodox religion?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, where did you live up until 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: In Zagreb, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were you educated in Croatia as well?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What education did you receive?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: The catering school in Zagreb, and I am a caterer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you perform military service with the Yugoslav national army in 1969 and 1970?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Raska. I did my military service in Raska, in the south of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And are you in fact married with two sons?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, did you and your family leave Croatia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, we did, all of us together.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Why did you leave?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Because of the situation as it was then. My wife was a born Belgrader, so there were these verbal provocations in terms of both my wife and my children, and that's why we decided to leave and to go and stay with her parents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And so you went to Belgrade at the end of 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, in December, late December. My wife and children were already in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Between eight and nine months in 1992. Until September, to be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could go briefly into private session. It won't be for long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, turning to the time that you spent in Djakovica, Kosovo, did you ever have problems with your Albanian colleagues or your Albanian neighbours?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know if the Albanian population had problems with the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If you can, could you briefly describe what kind of problems they were having.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Perhaps I won't define things properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's fine. We can move on to the next question.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Anyway, they were neglected sort of.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, just to be clear, who was neglected?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: The Albanians by the then-authorities. The authorities were predominantly Serb, although the Serbs were the minority population then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, can you describe the atmosphere in Djakovica in the spring of 1998? Had anything changed from previous years?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Nothing changed for me personally, but then you read the newspapers and you watch TV, and that's how I found out that all sorts of things started happening. Perhaps I can say provocations by Albanians against the Serbs. In Djakovica itself, it wasn't the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When did you first hear about the Kosovo Liberation Army? Approximately.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: I think it was that year, 1998. I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was it before the events that you will describe here today?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, before them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to be real specific, I know it's a long time ago, but was it a few months before then or can you estimate?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, a few months before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And what had you heard, if you can remember anything in particular.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, people were saying that they were armed, that they were ambushing Serb civilians, opposing the authorities and the military, things like that. That is mostly what people said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't intend to go into private session many times during this examination, but there are a couple of topics that I will ask that for. Can we go into private session again very briefly, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, you've said that on the 29th of June, 1998, you and your family were heading to Belgrade. How were you going to travel that day, by what mode of transportation?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Myself, my wife, and one of my sons, because the other one was a student of English literature in Pristina and he had already gone to Belgrade a day earlier, so as I said, my wife, my younger son and myself went there by bus because that was the only way to go there. We went to Belgrade via Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Who was on this bus that you took to Pristina -- or in the direction of Pristina, I should say.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Passengers. All of them travelled for their own reasons. I didn't know any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember if there were any Serbs on the bus besides yourself and your family?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. There were a few of them. I don't remember the exact number. I know that there were two girls and maybe two or three young men. I couldn't tell you the exact number. The bus was nearly full.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And were the rest of the people on the bus Albanian?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, they were Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know if the bus driver himself was Albanian or if he was Serb?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: He was Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember if there were any delays near the beginning of your trip after leaving Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. En route to Prizren, halfway there, the bus stopped because of a -- something broke down, and we waited there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I would like to use the ELMO. I'd like to put map 4 from Prosecution Exhibit P1 on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, you may be able to see it on the screen, but also to your left you have a map. It may be easier to see to your left. I'll leave it up to you. First, could you point out to the Trial Chamber where Djakovica is.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And is that where you were living with your family at the time?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. That's where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember what route the bus was supposed to take on that day, the 29th of June, 1998, to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: It was supposed to go via Prizren and Suva Reka and then on to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could you indicate that route as approximately as you can to the Trial Chamber using the map to your left.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Had you travelled to Pristina by bus on other occasions before that day?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps a month and a half before that day, because my wife was in hospital in Pristina, and I went there either by my company car or by bus, but I didn't take this particular route.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Which route did you take, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: We took a different route. That was the route that was always used if you wanted to go to Pristina and then on to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could you show that to the Trial Chamber on the map to your left, please, with the pointer that you have.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: I will try. [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that's clear to us.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: I don't know whether I got it right, but this is the general route.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know why that route was not taken on the 29th of June, 1998?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. It was said that that route was blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember who said that?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: That's what they said at the station, that that route was not safe, that it should not be taken, that a different route via Brezice should be taken if you wanted to go to Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think I'd like to show you one more map, and it's map 5 from Prosecution Exhibit P1. And if we could have that placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, what time should I be aiming for in terms of a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Because of the delay, there will have to be two shorter sessions. Quarter to or ten to 6.00 would be the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I don't know if it will be easier on this map or the prior one, but are you able to indicate more or less this route through Brezice that you just mentioned, on the map?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: I will try, but I'm not really familiar with those roads and routes, but they said that this route was via Brezice. I myself had never taken that particular road. [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the bus driver take this route through Brezice that you've just indicated to us?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Partly. Up until Suva Reka, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And where did he go after Suva Reka, if you could show us on the map, please.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And for the record, could it just show that he's continuing northwards up to Dule on that road. I think we're finished with the map. Thank you. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, did anyone ask the bus driver why he was taking this route through Dule instead of the route through Brezice?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. The ticket collector did and another man.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And did you hear the response to that question?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that he had asked the police and that the police had assured him that there was no shooting there. He had asked the police at the checkpoint as we were going out of Suva Reka. He asked them whether there was any shooting in Dule.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was the bus driver speaking in Serbian when he said this?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, at any point during your trip did you see soldiers along the road? After Suva Reka, I should clarify.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. Just before the bus was stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And were these KLA soldiers that you saw?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. The driver said, "Well, you see, this is the KLA."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you also see them with your own eyes? I'm just not clear.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. They were sitting on a meadow above the road. And the Albanian people started waving at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Is this the first time that you personally had ever seen the KLA or KLA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I'd like you just to describe what happened next after you saw those soldiers along the side of the road.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Perhaps a kilometre or two, I'm not really sure, further down the road the bus was stopped by three persons. One of the persons held the stop sign, something like that, and indicated with the stop sign to the bus that it should stop. This person was wearing a camouflage uniform with a cap with the KLA insignia on it. There were two other men there standing at the side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did the bus in fact stop?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: This plan with the stop sign entered the bus and asked to see our identification in Serbian. Our personal identification. Since my wife, my son, and myself, we sat right in the front, he first took my documents, checked them, and told me to get out. Then he checked Ivan's papers - that's my son - checked his documents and told him to get out too. We got out. My wife started crying and screaming. At one point she tried to seize my son, grab him, but one of the men standing out there pushed her roughly and threatened her, said to her in a threatening manner to calm down. There was an uproar. Two other people got off the bus at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could I interrupt you for just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Apparently my client is having some difficulty understanding the translators. They may be speaking a bit rapidly. If they could slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could try and assist there, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, as you know, everything we're saying is being translated into other languages, so if we can try to go slowly and speak as clearly as possible, it would be appreciated. Thank you. I believe you were just telling us whether or not anyone was asked off the bus besides you and your son. Did anyone else have to leave the bus?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. Two other young men got off the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What were their names?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: I learned their names later. I did not know them at the time, but I can tell their names now because I do know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please do tell their names.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: That was Zeljko Cuk and Stamen Genov.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please describe the one named Stamen Genov, how he looked then.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: He was a young man some 20 years of age, well-built. He was not as tall as I am, but he was really well-built young man, healthy, in his prime. Cuk was thin, taller than Genov. He was a real refugee, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, just to have a clear record, how tall are you in centimetres?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: 175 centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to show a couple of photos on the Sanction. They'll come up on your screen, Mr. Bakrac. These are from Prosecution Exhibit P54. That exhibit is under seal, but these pick photos are public. The first photo I'd like to show bears the ERN U0032164. Mr. Bakrac, do you recognise the person in the photo on your screen?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. That is Cuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did he look any different at the time that you saw him than he does in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Perhaps his hair was a bit longer, but his hair was sparse.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another photograph. For the record, it bears the ERN U0032165. Mr. Bakrac, do you recognise this person?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise him as Stamen Genov, but he's very young in this photograph. But you can see his facial features are already apparent in this young man.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we're done with this Sanction screen for the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, what happened when the four of you were taken off of the bus?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: When they took us off the bus, they took us across the road to a space between a shop and another building. They lined us up there. The man that had checked our documents said that Cuk, Genov, and Ivan should go first, in fact, that Genov and Ivan should go first and Cuk and I should remain there. And I begged them to let me stay with my son. He agreed and took Cuk and Genov in a car, a blue car. He took them away. I didn't know where he had taken them. Ivan and myself remained there. The third man who was an older man --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. I just want to ask you a couple of questions about what you just told us. Do you know what kind of car it was that Cuk and Genov were taken away in, the blue car that you say?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: I know that it was a blue car. I don't know if it was a Kadet or a Golf model. It's possible either way. At that time, I thought it was a Golf.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You also mentioned the soldier who had checked your documents. Do you remember anything about the other soldiers that had stopped the bus?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. One of them was a younger man with unkempt hair. He had some kind of a mark or a scar on his face. I think it was rather some kind of a mark, a deep pigmentation. The third man was tall, an older man, 50, 60 years of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Were these men armed?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, they were armed. The older man carried a rifle. It was a semi-automatic rifle. And the younger man had an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: At the time you were taken off the bus, I'd like to ask you a couple of questions about your status and that of the other three people taken off of the bus. Sir, were you armed at this time?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, we were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm focusing just on you. What were you wearing?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: I was wearing blue trousers, just a pair of normal shoes, and a yellow checked shirt with blue stripes, blue design on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, were you part of any military or police force at that time?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about your son Ivan? Was he armed at this time?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, not at that time, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What was he wearing when you were taken off the bus?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Jeans and the kind of shirt that young people wear. I don't know if there was any kind of a -- any kind of lettering on it. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How old was your son at this time?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: He had just turned 19 in August, the 16th of August. In fact, at that time he was not 19 yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was your son part of any military or police force?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was he paid by any military or police force to do anything?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, not at any time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The person you name as Cuk, was he armed when you were taken off of the bus?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: I don't think so. No, he didn't have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember what he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know if he was part of any military or police force?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: I don't know. I wouldn't say so. He was a refugee from -- I don't recall the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about Stamen Genov? Do you recall what he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: No, I don't remember, but everybody was in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Was he armed?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: I learned later that he did have a gun on the bus, a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: At any time during these events when you were being taken off the bus did he draw his weapon?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know what he did with the weapon?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: I learnt that after we were released, that he had left his satchel on the bus and that there was a firearm in that bag or satchel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know if Stamen Genov was a member of the police or the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: He was a member of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you learn what his rank in the military was?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. He was a sergeant in the medical corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, you yourself served in the JNA. What does one have to do to become a sergeant?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: You have to graduate from the secondary school, military secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know if Stamen Genov was married?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: I don't know if he was married at the time or perhaps he was supposed to get married soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: I learnt that after we were released, because a friend of mine, his wife's sister was his fiancee. I did know her, but I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning back to what you were describing to us earlier, were you guarded while Genov and Cuk were driven away?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. This older man stood guard over us, about a few metres away from us. We were sitting next to a wall on the ground. At one point I asked him if it was okay for us to smoke, and he said it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did this soldier have a weapon while he guarded you?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. He had a semi-automatic rifle with the implement for rifle launch grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Other than allowing you to have a cigarette, did this soldier say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. He told us about Greater Albania and things like that, and that he could kill us, throw our bodies away, and tell everybody that we had tried to escape but that he wouldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How were you feeling at this time?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How about your son? What was his reaction? Take your time. We can take a moment if you like.

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: My son was terribly frightened. He thought that he would be killed, just like me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did a car eventually come to pick up you and your son?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps it was within half an hour's time. I don't know exactly, but they did come back for the two of us eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: As far as we were concerned, we were taken in an unknown direction. It's only when we arrived that we realised where we had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And where was that? Where had you arrived, if you can describe the building or the room?

utterances.speaker: VOJKO BAKRAC
utterances.text: It was a village. I can put it that way. There was a building there. It had some kind of a fence around it. Perhaps I could put it this way: It was like a school, like a village school.
